A model\'s resolution is the size of each computational grid cell. The finer it is, the better the model captures local phenomena like convective showers, terrain effects or sea breezes. But this comes at a cost: very high-resolution models are expensive to run and their forecast horizon is short.
Rule of thumb: regional models describe more local detail at short lead times, while global models cover longer horizons. A finer grid alone does not guarantee a better forecast.

Compare several weather models to better understand convergence, divergence, and uncertainty.
MeteoCompare brings together several weather-model families so their signals can be compared instead of relying on a single source.
For numeric variables, the app applies four complementary approaches depending on context, local history, and the spread between models.
Robust agreement across models to extract a central value and a plausible range.
Adjusts some local historical biases when enough archive data is available.
Highlights several plausible evolutions instead of a single averaged value.
Dynamically combines the other three engines depending on context and data quality.

The displayed condition prioritizes native WMO weather codes: when at least two independent model families provide them, only those codes enter the consensus. Otherwise, one condition is derived from the central precipitation, temperature, and cloud-cover values.
The engine then distinguishes clear, mainly clear, partly cloudy, overcast, or foggy conditions from the available signals.
Rainy or wintry situations are grouped first, then resolved between rain, drizzle, snow, freezing rain, showers, or thunderstorms.
This hierarchical consensus reduces the bias of a simple categorical vote and prevents an isolated category from dominating unfairly.
MeteoCompare shows when models converge, but also when they diverge, so confidence and uncertainty stay readable.
When models tell a similar story, MeteoCompare shows tighter ranges and higher confidence.
When models split apart, the app makes the spread visible and calls attention to uncertainty.
In the very short term, radar complements the models to track the current observation and project the likely evolution of rain cells.
Radar is a short-term support tool to better anticipate immediate rain evolution.
The goal is to help compare scenarios, synthesise them, and step back before making a weather-related decision.
Clear aggregation of the best available forecasts.
Advanced algorithms condense the useful signals into readable guidance.
Visualise agreements, gaps, and confidence levels to take a step back.
MeteoCompare is a weather-analysis support tool. It highlights convergence and divergence between models, but it does not replace human expertise.
